title: The Footballer Who Gave Up the Game — A Decade of Foul-Smelling Stools and a Body Swelling From Within

sections.heading: The Patient's Story
sections.content:
He is a 26-year-old man from North East India, an avid footballer and keen farmer, presenting with six months of whole-body swelling. He had been entirely normal until age 15, when he first noticed a change in his bowel habits: large-volume, bulky, intensely foul-smelling stools with a consistency he likened to sputum or thick nasal discharge — sticky enough that it took several buckets of water to clear. He occasionally had a poorly localized deep ache with defecation that resolved instantly once he passed stool, though he never recalled seeing blood. These symptoms were sporadic and erratic at first, without fatigue, breathlessness, back pain, joint pain, facial puffiness, or leg swelling at that stage.

Over the following six years his symptoms worsened and he began losing weight, his clothes growing loose, even though his appetite remained strong — at times voracious. He couldn't pinpoint which foods triggered his symptoms, but noted that eating rotis, the household staple, often brought bloating and discomfort followed by large, foul-smelling stools; he switched to rice as his staple roughly a decade ago. By age 21 his weight loss and a sense of declining strength led him to retire from football, and farming and a stint as a light decorator both fell away as his interest waned.

His mother had similar symptoms for 20 years that reportedly resolved with herbal medicine, and he tried the same route two years ago — but his symptoms worsened instead, with bloating and the return of large, bulky stools. He denied jaundice, fatigue, loss of appetite, breathlessness, or palpitations at that time, though he did notice occasional nighttime diarrhea around 2–3 am. Multiple doctors and courses of medication brought little relief.

Over the last six months he developed early-morning facial swelling, followed by swelling in his legs and abdominal distension. He had frothy urine for about a week, a year ago, but denies blood in his urine, painful urination, or changes in urine volume. The swelling has been steadily progressing over these six months. He has an older sister and younger brother with no notable medical history. He previously drank alcohol and smoked marijuana for a period, without symptom relief. He has no known diabetes, hypertension, asthma, epilepsy, or thyroid disease.

sections.heading: What the Work-Up Showed So Far
sections.content:
- **General exam:** conscious, coherent, cooperative, thin build and nourishment; temperature 98.2°F, blood pressure 110/80 mmHg, pulse 82 bpm regular, respiratory rate 20/min, random blood glucose 132 mg/dL; no pallor, icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, or koilonychia; bilateral pitting pedal edema and facial puffiness present
- **Systemic exam:** heart sounds normal without added sounds; bilateral air entry with normal vesicular breath sounds; no focal neurological deficit
- **Abdominal exam:** soft and distended, with tenderness at the umbilical region, shifting dullness, and normal bowel sounds
- **Blood counts:** hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, total leukocyte count 5,000 cells/cu.mm, PCV 35.6, MCV 79.0 fl, MCH 26.9 pg, MCHC 34.5, platelets 2.97 lakh/cu.mm, RBC 4.56 million/cu.mm; smear showed normocytic normochromic red cells with adequate white cells and platelets
- **Urinalysis:** trace albumin, no sugar, 3–6 pus cells/HPF, 2–3 epithelial cells/HPF, no red cells; random blood sugar 101 mg/dL
- **Liver function:** total bilirubin 0.62 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.13 mg/dL, AST 101 IU/L, ALT 127 IU/L, ALP 190 IU/L, total protein markedly low at 2.3 g/dL, albumin 1.7 g/dL, A/G ratio 3.11
- **Renal function and electrolytes:** urea 13 mg/dL, creatinine 0.6 mg/dL, uric acid 5.3 mg/dL, calcium 7.7 mg/dL, sodium 137 mEq/L, potassium 3.5 mEq/L, chloride 106 mEq/L, phosphorus 2.3 mg/dL
- **Stool studies:** occult blood positive; no ova or parasites seen on initial examination
- **Imaging:** chest X-ray, ECG, and contrast-enhanced CT abdomen were performed

**Working diagnosis at admission:** chronic malabsorption with maldigestion, with inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, and autoimmune enteropathy considered as possible causes.

sections.heading: How the Story Unfolded on the Ward
sections.content:
He was started on IV thiamine and B-complex supplementation along with oral rehydration solution after each episode of loose stool, with regular vital sign monitoring. Over the following days his diarrhea fluctuated dramatically in frequency — from a handful of episodes some days to as many as 15 episodes in a single day — accompanied at times by mild diffuse abdominal tenderness and pedal edema that extended up to his knees. Working impressions during this period cycled between inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's or celiac-type), autoimmune enteropathy, and eventually protein-losing enteropathy given his markedly low total protein and albumin.

He underwent bowel preparation and had upper GI endoscopy and colonoscopy performed, with biopsy samples sent and results awaited; his working diagnosis at that point shifted toward suspected celiac disease. Symptomatic treatment continued with vitamin D supplementation, protein powder, anti-diarrheal agents (racecadotril and loperamide), and continued oral rehydration.

His diarrhea gradually settled — from ten episodes overnight to a few, then to resolution over the following days, with his stools eventually returning to a normal, pale-colored consistency. At that point, stool microscopy findings prompted the team to add giardiasis to the differential alongside suspected celiac disease, with a plan to start metronidazole or tinidazole pending confirmation. By the final documented update, the working diagnosis had settled on giardiasis as a likely contributor to his longstanding malabsorption, though the biopsy results to confirm or exclude celiac disease remained pending.
